articles.standfirst: He joined the band as bassist in 2021, following the death of Dusty Hill
articles.summary: He joined the band as bassist in 2021, following the death of Dusty Hill
articles.body:
Frank Beard , original drummer of the Texas trio ZZ Top , died on Tuesday at the age of 77 at his ranch in Richmond , Texas, after a long musical career spanning more than half a century.

"Today, Elwood (Francis) and I lost a great friend and collaborator, and the world lost one of the most naturally innovative drummers and a great and true son of Texas," wrote Billy Gibbons , the band's singer and guitarist, on social media.

Francis is not part of the original trio, as he joined the band as bassist in 2021 , following the death of Dusty Hill , the third original member of this band.

For his part, Gibbons also highlighted Beard's "signature 'backbeat'" (a rhythmic accent placed on the weak beats of a measure), stating that it was key "to keeping ZZ Top at the top" .

The group, formed in 1969 in Houston by Billy Gibbons , Dusty Hill , and Beard himself, was known for combining an unmistakable Texan boogie blues rock sound with a visual image of long beards, dark glasses, and hats.

' Beard , whose last name means "beard" in English, was, ironically, the only member of the trio without a long beard and, instead, wore a mustache, a contrast that the band exploited humorously on several occasions.'

Over more than five decades with ZZ Top , Beard ’s rhythm was the foundation of some of Texas rock’s biggest hits, such as "La Grange," "Tush," "Sharp Dressed Man," and "Legs," among others.

With him on drums, the band sold more than 50 million records , landed six singles at number one on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Airplay chart, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

articles.title: Ariana Grande lashes out at Trump for using one of her songs in a political video: "Never use my music again"
articles.standfirst: He used ‘We Can’t Be Friends’ in a video with a message against trans people
articles.summary: He used ‘We Can’t Be Friends’ in a video with a message against trans people
articles.body:
Ariana Grande has once again publicly confronted the Donald Trump Administration after the official Team Trump account used one of her songs to accompany a political message. This time it was ‘We Can’t Be Friends (Wait For Your Love)’, one of the singer’s biggest hits released in 2024, which appeared as the soundtrack to a video with a message against trans people.

The video, posted on Thursday on TikTok, shows Donald Trump walking toward a podium while phrases appear on screen that begin with a reference to Grande’s song and end with the message: " Men cannot have babies and should never compete in women’s sports." The post also added the message “This should not be controversial” alongside Trump and MAGA tags.

Grande responded directly in the post's comments with a forceful message: “ Never use my music again . Also, your truth is false.” The video now appears without sound, after the singer's team worked to get the song removed.

It’s not the first time Ariana Grande has protested against Trump

The clash between the singer and the Trump Administration goes back a few weeks. In June, the White House used ‘ Bye ’, another Grande song, in a TikTok video about U.S. immigration policy.

The post showed images of agents from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement Service (ICE) detaining and handcuffing people and carried the message: “Bye-bye. President Trump has achieved the safest border in history.” Grande then responded by asking that her music no longer be used in connection with that kind of content .

Following that protest, the audio was removed from the video, although the post remained available. The White House then responded to Grande's criticism by defending its immigration policy.

A long list of musicians opposed to Trump

Ariana Grande is not the only artist who has publicly asked Trump and his team to stop using their songs. Taylor Swift, Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, SZA, Katy Perry, Céline Dion, ABBA, the Rolling Stones, and Noah Kahan , among others, have also protested at different times over the use of their music being associated with Trump’s political messages or events.

The issue also has a legal dimension that is not always as straightforward as it seems. Political campaigns may have general licenses from organizations such as ASCAP or BMI to play certain songs at public events, but the use of a song within a video posted on social media raises different issues, especially when it involves synchronizing a recording with images and political messages .

That is why, when an artist publicly says they do not want a politician to use their music, it does not automatically mean that there is a copyright infringement in every case. It depends on what rights have been obtained, who owns the work, and how the recording has been used.

In Ariana Grande's case, however, the practical outcome of this latest episode has already occurred: the Team Trump video has lost the song that accompanied it.

articles.title: Janie Bradford Hobbs net worth: What was the net worth of the Motown legend who died at 87?
articles.standfirst: She contributed to some of the most influential songs in music history
articles.summary: She contributed to some of the most influential songs in music history
articles.body:
The music world is mourning the loss of Janie Bradford Hobbs, one of the pioneering figures behind Motown Records whose songwriting helped shape the sound of an era.

Bradford Hobbs died at age 87 following an extended illness, her family confirmed over the weekend. While her name may not have been as widely recognized as the artists who performed her songs, her impact on American music was immense.

Janie Bradford Hobbs' estimated net worth

Although no official financial records have been made public, celebrity wealth estimates and industry analyses have generally placed Janie Bradford Hobbs' net worth between $2 million and $5 million at the time of her death. The estimate reflects decades of royalty earnings, publishing rights, executive work within Motown, and her contributions to some of the most influential songs in music history.

Unlike many modern artists who generate wealth through touring, endorsements, and social media ventures, Bradford Hobbs built her financial legacy through songwriting and music publishing, areas that can provide long-term royalty income for decades after a song's release.

The song that helped launch Motown

Bradford Hobbs' most famous contribution came when she co-wrote "Money (That's What I Want)" alongside Motown founder Berry Gordy. Recorded by Barrett Strong in 1959, the song became one of Motown's earliest commercial successes and helped establish the label as a major force in American music.

Its influence extended far beyond its original release. The song was later covered by numerous artists, including The Beatles, ensuring that it continued generating attention, and likely royalty income, for generations. That single composition alone secured Bradford Hobbs a place in music history.

A catalog filled with legendary artists

Her success was not limited to one song. Bradford Hobbs also wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby," which eventually became one of Marvin Gaye's signature hits. Throughout her career, she contributed songs recorded by some of the biggest names in Motown history, including Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas, and The Temptations.

Few songwriters can claim credits connected to such a remarkable collection of artists. Because publishing royalties often continue for decades, her catalog likely remained a meaningful source of income long after her active songwriting years ended.

From receptionist to Motown architect

Bradford Hobbs' story is one of the most remarkable in Motown history.

Born in Charleston, Missouri, she later moved to Detroit , where a connection through singer Jackie Wilson introduced her to Berry Gordy in the late 1950s.

She initially joined the company as a receptionist in 1958. But Motown was still in its infancy, and employees often wore multiple hats. Bradford Hobbs quickly became involved in the creative side of the business and soon emerged as one of the label's most important early contributors.

Berry Gordy highlighted that role in his statement following her death.

"Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown , and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said. He also described her as one of the "original Motown family" members who helped build the company before it became a global phenomenon.

articles.title: Why Dolly Parton was considered the greatest Country artist of all time
articles.standfirst: She was a woman whose influence reached far beyond the music charts
articles.summary: She was a woman whose influence reached far beyond the music charts
articles.body:
The world of music lost one of its brightest stars when news broke that Dolly Parton had passed away at the age of 80. Her death marks the end of an extraordinary career that spanned nearly six decades and transformed country music and American popular culture.

For many fans, artists, and industry executives, Parton's place among country music's elite had long been beyond debate. But in November 2024, Billboard officially settled the argument for many observers when it ranked Parton No. 1 on its list of the 100 Greatest Country Artists of All Time, placing her ahead of legends such as Johnny Cash, Hank Williams, George Jones, Loretta Lynn, Willie Nelson, and Merle Haggard.

Parton reacted to the honor with the same humility and charm that defined her public persona throughout her life. "I just learned that Billboard Magazine just released their list of greatest country artists of all time, and they have my name sitting at the top! Can you believe that?" she said in a video message to fans.

Now, less than two years later, that recognition carries even greater significance as the music world reflects on the legacy of a woman whose influence reached far beyond the country charts.

A career unlike any other

When Dolly released her debut album, Hello, I'm Dolly, in 1967, few could have predicted the impact she would have on the genre. Over the next several decades, she built one of the most impressive résumés in music history. She scored 25 No. 1 hits on Billboard's Country Songs chart, more than any other female artist. Her catalog included 49 top-10 country albums and nine No. 1 albums, a remarkable achievement that stretched across generations of listeners.

What made those accomplishments even more remarkable was her longevity. Parton continued to find success well into her seventies, with her 2023 album Rockstar introducing her to new audiences and demonstrated that she remained a creative force long after most performers would have retired.

The songwriter who defined generations

Parton's greatest gift may have been her songwriting. Few artists in any genre have written songs with the emotional power and cultural staying power of classics such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "I Will Always Love You," "9 to 5," and "Here You Come Again." Her songs told stories that felt deeply personal while remaining universally relatable and touched topics such as about poverty, heartbreak, family, ambition, or faith. Parton had an unmatched ability to connect with listeners.

"I Will Always Love You" alone would have secured her place in music history. Written by Parton in 1973 and later transformed into one of the best-selling singles ever by Whitney Houston, the song became a global phenomenon while introducing millions of listeners to Parton's songwriting brilliance.

Unlike many performers who rely on outside writers, Parton built much of her legacy through her own pen, giving her a level of artistic authenticity that resonated with generations of country fans.

A bridge between country and popular culture

Parton also accomplished something few country artists have managed: she became a global icon without abandoning her roots. She grew up listening to country legends such as Hank Williams, Kitty Wells, and Johnny Cash, dreaming of one day performing on the Grand Ole Opry.

Those influences shaped her music, but she also expanded the reach of country music by crossing into film, television, pop music, and business.

Through movies like 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias , as well as countless television appearances, Parton became one of the most recognizable entertainers in the world.

However, she never stopped being identified as a country artist. Her success helped bring country music to audiences who might never have otherwise embraced the genre, making her one of its most important ambassadors. When Billboard assembled its ranking of the 100 Greatest Country Artists of All Time , editors considered more than chart performance. They evaluated artistry, longevity, cultural influence, and an artist's ability to move the genre forward.

She remained relevant across six decades, influenced countless performers, and continuously reinvented herself while staying true to her identity. Artists ranging from Reba McEntire and Shania Twain to Taylor Swift, Kacey Musgraves, and Lainey Wilson have cited Parton as an inspiration. Her impact extended beyond music as well. She became known for her philanthropy, literacy initiatives, and charitable efforts, earning admiration even among people who were not country music fans.

articles.title: Bad Bunny suffers major financial loss despite winning legal copyright fight in court
articles.standfirst: The multi-million dollar music artist will have to fork out a big chunk of change now.
articles.summary: The multi-million dollar music artist will have to fork out a big chunk of change now.
articles.body:
For a very long time, practically since the release of his debut studio album " X 100pre ", Bad Bunny has done nothing but win and win big. He continues to break records of all kinds, and only seems to be getting better at 32 years old .

But eventually, he was going to have to deal with some sort of setback. That's just the nature of the game, although this time it came in a somewhat unexpected manner: in the courtroom of all places . Yet his loss came after he actually got another win .

Bad Bunny's legal team was recently put to work due to a copyright lawsuit waged on the music artist's team . The song " Enséñame a Bailar " from his iconic " Un Verano Sin Ti " album was claimed to have used a sample from Nigerian music artist Dera 's song, " Empty My Pocket ", without permission.

Empawa Africa Music Services Limited filed the lawsuit in May of 2025, only to drop it later once it was confirmed that Bad Bunny's team had properly cleared the sample through one of the copyright holders, Lakizo Entertainment .

Bad Bunny forced to pay over $465,000 in legal fees stemming from copyright lawsuit

But even though Bad Bunny won the lawsuit, his legal team sought reimbursement for the $465,615 in legal fees the lawsuit ended up costing.

That follow-up legal battle didn't pan out as expected for Bad Bunny. The judge ultimately ruled that the initial lawsuit was "objectively reasonable", and that making Empawa pay for all of the legal costs would be "strongly antithetical" .

Bad Bunny is now on the hook for that chunk of change , although given his incredible fortune - which is only growing - he should be able to withstand the financial hit.

articles.title: Taylor Swift looks radiant wearing her wedding ring during her first performance since marrying Travis Kelce
articles.standfirst: The pop superstar returned to the stage with a nostalgic piano medley while proudly displaying her new wedding band
articles.summary: The pop superstar returned to the stage with a nostalgic piano medley while proudly displaying her new wedding band
articles.body:
T aylor Swift gave fans their first close look at her wedding ring during her first public performance since marrying Travis Kelce , adding another personal detail to an appearance that already celebrated two decades of her career.

The 36-year-old singer appeared at the Grammy Museum for “The Icon Sessions with Taylor Swift: A 20-Year Retrospective,” an intimate event presented by the Recording Academy's Songwriters & Composers Wing.

The August 18 gathering combined a conversation about Swift's career with a rare live performance.

Swift performed at the piano, delivering a medley that included “I Knew It, I Knew You,” “August” and “All Too Well.” The performance was particularly notable because it marked her first public performance since her July wedding to Kelce at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

As she played, cameras captured the singer's ring stack, including her new wedding band alongside the old mine cut diamond engagement ring designed by Kindred Lubeck.

The wedding band immediately attracted attention because it was one of the clearest public views yet of the jewelry Swift received as part of her marriage.

Swift kept the rest of her appearance elegant and understated. She wore a sheer sage-green Dôen dress featuring a deep-red shoulder embellishment, complemented by pendant earrings, an updo with her familiar bangs and berry-toned lipstick.

The jewelry and styling gave the performance an unmistakably personal quality, particularly because Swift has spent much of her career turning major life moments into parts of her public artistic narrative.

Her appearance also came with a candid discussion about the less glamorous side of being one of the world's most recognizable entertainers.

Swift reflects on fame, music and life after the wedding

During a conversation with Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr., Swift discussed how she manages the pressures that have accompanied her extraordinary level of fame.

“I go through several processes and coping mechanisms that I’ve gone through over the years,” she said. “And one of them is saying, ‘You chose this. You chose this every day. You could have opted out of this any day before it got unmanageably big.’ And I decided not to because I love it that much.”

“Everything that comes with this ultimately is worth it as long as I get to still make music,” she added.

Those comments offered an interesting backdrop to her return to performing. Swift's wedding has generated enormous attention, but the Grammy Museum appearance placed the emphasis back on the part of her life that has defined her career: songwriting and performing.

Swift and Kelce married on July 3 at Madison Square Garden following months of intense speculation.

The couple's representatives confirmed the ceremony after the venue's exterior screens displayed “JUST&T MARRIED!” The wedding was officiated by Adam Sandler , while Swift's brother Austin served as her “man of honor” and Kelce's brother Jason was his best man.

Both Swift and Kelce wore Christian Dior designs created by Jonathan Anderson, with Swift also wearing Cartier jewelry and Christian Louboutin shoes.

Since the ceremony, the newlyweds have largely been seen attending celebrations with friends.

Their first appearance as husband and wife came at JuJu Smith-Schuster and Laura Kruk's wedding on July 10, while Swift was later spotted at another wedding in the U.K. on August 15 alongside Sabrina Carpenter and Jack Antonoff.

The Grammy Museum performance therefore represented something different: Swift returning to the stage, surrounded by her music and career history, while quietly acknowledging the biggest change in her personal life.

With her wedding band now clearly visible beside her engagement ring, the performance offered fans a glimpse of Swift entering a new chapter while continuing to do what she has always done best: make music.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's secret that led to her death has been revealed
articles.standfirst: New details explain the health struggles that forced the singer to scale back appearances in her final weeks
articles.summary: New details explain the health struggles that forced the singer to scale back appearances in her final weeks
articles.body:
Dolly Parton had spoken publicly about difficult health problems in the final weeks of her life, but one crucial detail remained private: the country music icon was also battling cancer.

Parton died August 25 at age 80 at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, surrounded by loved ones, according to a statement from her representatives. They confirmed that cancer was behind her death but didn't disclose the specific type she had been diagnosed with.

“After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” her representatives said.

The announcement provided new context for a series of health concerns that had become increasingly visible in the days before her death.

Parton had reportedly been hospitalized five days earlier with kidney and autoimmune issues. She had also canceled a scheduled appearance at Dollywood after her doctor advised against traveling.

“Sometimes I get a little dizzy and I get dehydrated,” Parton explained in a prerecorded message. “And so my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, ‘You ain’t traveling this week.’”

Parton acknowledged ‘hard times’ with health

Just four days before her death, Parton spoke about her health in an interview with People, saying she had neglected some of her own medical needs while caring for her husband, Carl Dean , before his death in March 2025.

“It’s not like I haven’t been through hard times with my health,” she stated.

Despite those struggles, Parton continued making public appearances virtually. On August 19, she accepted the ACM Poet’s Award and reflected on the creative work that had defined her career.

“You know, I’ve been able to do many things throughout my life, but at my core, songwriting has always been the most important part of who I am creatively,” Parton said.

Her representatives’ statement also emphasized the legacy she built away from the stage, including the millions of books distributed through her Imagination Library and her financial support for vaccine research.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched,” they said.

Family shares Parton’s final request

Her nephew and longtime head of security, Bryan Seaver , later announced her death on behalf of the family.

“This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality,” Seaver said. “It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness.”

He also revealed that Parton had asked to be laid to rest “in a beautiful bed of plush cotton.”

“After a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable,” Seaver added.

Tributes quickly followed from some of her longtime friends and co-stars. Julia Roberts , who appeared with Parton in Steel Magnolias, called her a “magical and joyous human,” adding, “The sun has dimmed today.”

Sally Field and Lily Tomlin were also among those honoring a performer whose influence stretched across music, film and philanthropy.

articles.title: Dolly Parton requested that this song be played at her funeral
articles.standfirst: The singer had already explained which gospel hymn she wanted at her farewell and why it mattered so much
articles.summary: The singer had already explained which gospel hymn she wanted at her farewell and why it mattered so much
articles.body:
Dolly Parton spent a lifetime writing songs that became part of other people’s milestones, heartbreaks and goodbyes. Long before her own death at 80, she had already decided which song she wanted to accompany her final farewell.

Parton revealed in a 2014 interview with Entertainment Weekly that she wanted “If We Never Meet Again” sung at her funeral, choosing a gospel hymn with a powerful connection to her father.

“There’s a song called ‘If We Never Meet Again,’” Parton said. “It’s an old country-gospel church song that talks about if we never meet again this side of heaven, I will meet you on that beautiful shore. ‘Where the charming roses bloom forever and where separations come no more.’”

The song wasn't simply one she admired. It had already been part of one of the most difficult moments of her life.

“That was my daddy’s favorite,” Parton said. “We did sing it at his funeral, and I would like it to be sung at mine.”

Written by Albert E. Brumley in 1945, the hymn has endured through generations and has been recorded by artists including Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash .

‘I Will Always Love You’ carried different kind meaning

Parton also knew there was another song audiences would associate with her death.

“I’m sure they’ll be playing ‘I Will Always Love You’ when I die, just like they did with Whitney Houston,” she said.

That thought came from an intensely emotional memory. Houston ’s soaring recording of the song became one of the biggest hits of her career after appearing in The Bodyguard, nearly two decades after Parton had written and recorded the original.

“When they picked her coffin up and started in on that song, I started to cry, and I thought, ‘Oh my Lord,’” Parton recalled. “That’s when it hit me that she was really gone.”

The song itself was originally written as a farewell to Porter Wagoner , as Parton prepared to leave their professional partnership and pursue her solo career.

Funeral plans reflect private side of her life

The details emerging after her death point toward an intimate farewell rather than a large public spectacle.

Her representatives said Parton had requested a small, private service for immediate family. Reports also indicated that she would be laid to rest beside her husband, Carl Dean , at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville.

Her nephew and longtime head of security, Bryan Seaver , revealed another characteristically personal request: Parton wanted to be laid to rest in “a beautiful bed of plush cotton.”

“After a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest,” Seaver said.

It's perhaps fitting that a woman whose public life was filled with rhinestones, stages and worldwide fame chose something so simple for her final music.

The song she wanted wasn't her biggest hit, but it was her father’s favorite.

articles.title: Why did Dolly Parton and husband, Carl Dean, decide not to have children?
articles.standfirst: Health struggles and career choices shaped one of the most personal decisions of her life
articles.summary: Health struggles and career choices shaped one of the most personal decisions of her life
articles.body:
Dolly Parton didn't begin married life assuming she would never have children. In fact, she and Carl Dean once talked about what their kids might look like, chose names and expected parenthood to become part of their future. It simply never happened.

Over the decades, Parton became increasingly open about that reality, explaining that she eventually made peace with it and came to believe that not becoming a mother allowed her to build the career and philanthropic legacy that defined much of her life.

“Early on, when my husband and I were dating, and then when we got married, we just assumed we would have kids,” Parton told Billboard in 2014.

“We weren’t doing anything to stop it. In fact, we thought maybe we would. We even had names if we did, but it didn’t turn out that way.”

Health struggles changed what was possible

Parton , one of 12 siblings, was already accustomed to caring for children. She helped look after younger brothers and sisters and later remained close to her nieces and nephews, who affectionately called her “Aunt Granny.”

Medical issues also became part of the story. She was diagnosed with endometriosis and later underwent a partial hysterectomy in the 1980s, leaving her unable to carry children naturally.

Parton later described the period following the operation as a deeply difficult one. Still, she and Dean continued to talk about the family they might have had.

“My husband and I, when we first got married, we thought about if we had kids, what would they look like?” Parton told the Guardian in 2014. “Would they be tall, because he’s tall? Or would they be little squats like me?

“We talked about it and we dreamed it, but it wasn’t meant to be.”

Motherhood may have changed her career

As she got older, Parton said she became increasingly convinced that motherhood would have pulled her in a very different direction.

“I would have been a great mother, I think,” she said. “I would probably have given up everything else because I would’ve felt guilty about that, if I’d have left them.

“Everything would have changed. I probably wouldn’t have been a star."

That perspective hardened into acceptance.

"The older we get, the gladder we are that we don’t have them now, because we take care of a lot of other people’s kids,” Parton told Rolling Stone in 2003.

Her relationship with children eventually became central to one of her biggest charitable projects. She launched the Imagination Library in 1995 to provide free books to young children, and the program has since distributed hundreds of millions of books worldwide.

“God has a plan for everything,” Parton said in 2017. “I think it probably was his plan for me not to have kids so everybody’s kids could be mine — and they are now.”

Parton and Dean remained married for 58 years until his death in 2025. By then, what had once been an unanswered question had become something Parton viewed as part of the life she was meant to lead.

articles.title: Dolly Parton left behind an enigmatic secret that will be revealed in 2045: it is a song she composed that will come to light in 19 years
articles.standfirst: The story dates back to 2015, when Parton inaugurated Dollywood's DreamMore Resort complex: she wrote and recorded an unreleased song that was stored in a wooden box
articles.summary: The story dates back to 2015, when Parton inaugurated Dollywood's DreamMore Resort complex: she wrote and recorded an unreleased song that was stored in a wooden box
articles.body:
The death of Dolly Parton this past Tuesday at the age of 80 leaves behind a career full of successes , but also a mystery that will remain hidden for nearly two more decades . The American artist recorded a secret song that will stay concealed until 2045, the year in which she would have turned 99 .

The story dates back to 2015, when Parton inaugurated Dollywood's DreamMore Resort complex in Tennessee. As part of a special initiative, she wrote and recorded an unreleased song that was stored in a wooden box along with a CD player , with instructions to not open it until 30 years later .

The singer always acknowledged that that decision cost her more than she imagined. "It's like burying one of my children," she even said about a song no one has heard and whose title she never revealed either. As the years went by, she confessed in several interviews that she would like to get it back because she considered it "a very good song".

When she accepted the challenge, many told her she probably wouldn’t live to hear it . Her response became famous over time: "Maybe I will. I’ll be 99 years old. I’ve seen people live longer than that" .

Now, after her death, that promise takes on a different dimension . Unless the established plans are changed, the song will remain under lock and key until 2045, becoming one of the most curious legacies and enigmatic ones left by the queen of country.

articles.title: The day Dolly Parton turned Dallas Cowboys' Thanksgiving halftime show into one of the NFL's best performances
articles.standfirst: At 77, the country icon turned a short NFL performance into one of the most talked-about moments of the holiday
articles.summary: At 77, the country icon turned a short NFL performance into one of the most talked-about moments of the holiday
articles.body:
Dolly Parton didn't need a Super Bowl-sized production to own an NFL stage. On Thanksgiving Day in 2023, she needed six minutes, four songs and one outfit that immediately became part of football folklore.

The country music icon stepped onto the field at AT&T Stadium during halftime of the Dallas Cowboys ’ game against the Washington Commanders wearing a sparkling version of the Cowboys cheerleader uniform in front of roughly 93,000 fans. The reaction was instant.

Parton opened with “Jolene,” followed with “9 to 5,” then closed with Queen’s “We Will Rock You” and “We Are the Champions,” both featured on her Rockstar album. It was a compact set, but nothing about it felt small.

Parton understood the moment

The outfit became the biggest talking point, but Parton later made clear that she understood the risk.

“I thought, ‘Well at my age, if I can pull it off, it’s going to be good. And if I don’t, I can just pass it off as an old woman doing a stupid ass thing,’” she told USA Today.

She added: “I’ve always said my desire to do something is greater than my fear of it.”

That attitude helped carry the performance when part of the staging reportedly failed. Parton was expected to rise through a silver star-shaped platform, but the mechanism did not function as planned. She simply kept going.

The crowd barely seemed to notice, and the show never lost momentum. The performance quickly became a national talking point, helped by CBS analyst Tony Romo , whose enthusiastic reaction on the broadcast spread across social media.

The timing was also perfect. Rockstar had been released only days earlier, and the Cowboys appearance gave Parton a massive platform to perform material tied to the album while also kicking off the Salvation Army’s annual Red Kettle Campaign .

Dallas then completed the afternoon with a dominant 45-10 victory over Washington, with Dak Prescott throwing four touchdown passes.

Still, by the end of the day, one of the biggest stories had happened during halftime.

Football connection felt natural

The Cowboys show wasn't Parton ’s only major football appearance that year. Days earlier, Peyton Manning escorted her onto the field at Neyland Stadium, where she performed “Rocky Top” during Tennessee’s game against Georgia.

“My East Tennessee roots run deep, and I am so proud to be partnering with the Vols,” Parton said at the time.

She had also worked with ESPN and the University of Tennessee on football-related projects, while the Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame had previously named her Tennessean of the Year.

That broader connection helps explain why the Cowboys performance still stands out years later.

It wasn't simply a celebrity cameo. It was Parton doing what she did throughout her career in taking a huge stage, leaning fully into the moment and making it feel unmistakably her own.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus' heart-wrenching tribute to "angel by my side" Dolly Parton has fans in tears
articles.standfirst: Parton was Cyrus' godmother and they had a very close relationship for many years.
articles.summary: Parton was Cyrus' godmother and they had a very close relationship for many years.
articles.body:
There has been no shortage of emotional tributes pouring in following the passing of Dolly Parton . And that will continue to be the case for a little while, as her impact on the world was nothing short of incredibly strong.

Those who were close to her are feeling her death more than anyone else. Iconic music artist Miley Cyrus is one of those people, given her lifelong relationship with Parton. As a dear friend to Billy Ray Cyrus , Parton became Miley's godmother when she was born in 1992 . As it turns out, Parton and Miley were actually related, as it was recently revealed that they were seventh cousins, once removed .

Miley Cyrus says one of her last conversations with Dolly Parton was about "music and metamorphosis"

Given their strong bond, Cyrus' tribute on social media was bound to be a heartfelt and emotional one. Cyrus took a day to gather her thoughts, and penned a heart-wrenching message to her departed godmother.

The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts. What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.

Fans poured into Cyrus' comment section to send loving words of their own. Some even mentioned that Cyrus was the gateway for young people to become accustomed to Parton's music . There's no doubt that this will be a wound that might never heal for many people, including Cyrus.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's sister reveals the singer's last wishes, including a surprising offer to her doctors
articles.standfirst: Dolly’s sister shares a remarkable detail about the singer’s final wishes following her private cancer battle
articles.summary: Dolly’s sister shares a remarkable detail about the singer’s final wishes following her private cancer battle
articles.body:
Dolly Parton’s final act of generosity may have been one of her most remarkable.

After the country music legend died at 80 on August 25 following a private battle with cancer, her sister Stella Parton revealed that Dolly had been prepared to help other patients even if her own treatment could no longer save her.

In a heartfelt tribute shared after her sister’s death, Stella described Dolly as one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people she’d ever known.

She also disclosed a conversation they’d had recently, saying Dolly told her that if doctors could no longer offer hope for her recovery, she’d still permit her medical team to try experimental drugs.

“My sister was one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people I’ve ever known,” wrote Stella on Facebook.

“What the world saw is exactly who she was, so much so, she told me recently that if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future.

“My sister was always thinking of others and if you want to honor her legacy, show more kindness, lift others up and give more of your time and resources as she continued to do to the very end.”

The revelation adds to Dolly’s final chapter. Her family confirmed that she’d been secretly battling cancer, though they haven’t publicly identified the type.

Reports also indicated that she’d been hospitalized at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville shortly before her death, reportedly dealing with kidney and autoimmune issues.

Dolly’s family is expected to honor her wishes with a small, private funeral service for immediate family members in Nashville.

Dolly’s music surges following her death

While Stella’s tribute has highlighted Dolly’s compassion, the singer’s extraordinary musical legacy has also received an enormous wave of attention since her passing.

Data from Luminate showed that streams of Dolly’s music in the United States surged from 1.2 million on August 24 to 26.3 million the following day. That represents an extraordinary 2,109% increase. Globally, her audio and video streams climbed 1,280%, rising from 2.5 million to 35 million.

“Jolene” experienced one of the biggest jumps, increasing from more than 196,000 streams to 2.7 million. “9 to 5” climbed to 2.3 million, while “Islands in the Stream,” her famous collaboration with the late Kenny Rogers, reached 1.8 million.

Dolly’s own recording of “I Will Always Love You” also saw renewed interest, reaching 1.7 million streams. The song was later transformed into a global smash by Whitney Houston , but its origins remained firmly rooted in Dolly’s songwriting.

Other songs receiving a major boost included “Here You Come Again,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “There Was Jesus,” “Why’d You Come In Here Lookin’ Like That?” and “My Tennessee Mountain Home.”

Her more recent collaboration with Beyoncé , “Tyrant,” also experienced a substantial increase.

Dolly Parton spent decades entertaining millions while using her success to make a difference. Even near the end of her life, her reported willingness to help future patients suggests that putting others first remained central to who she was.

articles.title: Dolly Parton obituary in Nashville leaves her family and fans in tears
articles.standfirst: The country music legend was remembered in deeply personal tributes from both her family and a Nashville funeral home.
articles.summary: The country music legend was remembered in deeply personal tributes from both her family and a Nashville funeral home.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton’s death has prompted an outpouring of grief, with a Nashville obituary and an emotional family statement capturing both her extraordinary public life and the private heartbreak surrounding her passing.

“Dolly Parton [was] known to the world as a beloved singer, songwriter, philanthropist, actress, playwright, and author,” the obituary read, noting that the country music icon “died peacefully” on 25 August in Nashville, Tennessee.

The tribute then summed up the warmth and personality that made Parton one of the most beloved entertainers of her generation.

“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family.”

Dolly Parton’s family shares emotional farewell

Her family also issued a deeply personal statement through her nephew, Seaver , who had served as Parton’s head of security for more than two decades.

“I am representing the Parton and Owens family today, announcing the passing of my Aunt Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean. Sister, sis, Aunt Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next,” Seaver began.

“This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now.”

Family reveals Dolly Parton’s final moments

The statement also confirmed that Parton had been battling cancer before her death.

“After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life [Tuesday] at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” the statement read in part.

Her relatives went on to emphasize the generosity and joy that defined Parton’s life away from the stage.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand.”
